glossary: Block grant
Federal money for a broad policy area with minimal restrictions on how states spend it. Preferred by the states.
Categorical grant
Federal money restricted to specific categories of spending. Preferred by the national government and the most commonly used form of federal aid.
Commandeering
The national government ordering state officials to carry out a federal program. The Court has held that Congress may not do this.
Concurrent powers
Powers held by both the national and state governments, such as collecting taxes, borrowing money, and making and enforcing laws.
Conditions of aid
Requirements attached to federal grants that states must meet in order to receive the money.
Confederation
A system in which sovereign states delegate limited authority to a weak central government. The Articles of Confederation created one.
Cooperative federalism
Marble cake federalism. National and state governments share responsibilities, with national funding and state administration blended together. Associated with the New Deal and after.
Cross-cutting requirement
A condition that applies to nearly all federal grants, such as a ban on discrimination.
Crossover sanction
Withholding federal money in one program to influence state policy in another area — for example, highway funds and the minimum drinking age.
Devolution
Shifting power and responsibility from the national government back to the states. The “devolution revolution” began in the 1980s and accelerated in the 1990s.
Dual federalism
Layer cake federalism. National and state governments operate in separate spheres. Dominant from the founding into the 1930s.
Entitlement
A program that guarantees benefits to everyone who meets its eligibility rules, such as Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
Enumerated powers
Powers written in the Constitution, mostly in Article I, Section 8. Also called expressed powers.
Every Student Succeeds Act (2015)
Replaced No Child Left Behind and returned more control over school accountability to the states.
Exclusive powers
Powers held by only one level of government. National exclusive powers include enumerated and implied powers.
Federal mandate
A requirement the national government places on state or local governments.
Federal system
A system in which power is divided between a national government and state governments, each with constitutional authority of its own.
Federalism
The system of government in the United States in which power is shared between the national and state governments.
Federalist No. 39

Madison’s essay arguing that the Constitution is “a composition of both” national and federal features. Remember: when Madison says “federal,” he means the states — not the national government. Required document.
Fiscal federalism
The national government’s use of grants and the conditions attached to them to influence state policy.
Fourteenth Amendment
Ratified in 1868. Its Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses give the national government power to enforce protections for individuals against the states.
Full faith and credit clause
Article IV. Requires each state to honor the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of every other state.
Implied powers
National powers not written in the Constitution but inferred from the Necessary and Proper Clause, such as creating a national bank.
Laboratories of democracy
The idea that states can try new policies on a small scale; failures stay contained and successes can be copied.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
Congress may create a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and a state may not tax it because of the Supremacy Clause. Required case.
Multiple access points
The many places — local, state, and national — where people and groups can try to influence policy. A result of federalism and separation of powers.
New Deal
Franklin Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression in the 1930s. It greatly expanded the national government’s role and began the era of cooperative federalism.
No Child Left Behind Act (2001)
Tied federal education funds to national testing and accountability requirements. Replaced by the Every Student Succeeds Act in 2015.
Police power
The states’ general authority to regulate for health, safety, welfare, and morals. The national government has no general police power.
Preemption
Federal law displacing state law on the same subject. Grounded in the Supremacy Clause.
Reserved powers
Powers not delegated to the national government, which the Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people.
Revenue sharing
Federal money given to states with almost no restrictions. The least used form of federal funding; it ran from 1972 to 1986.
Selective incorporation
The Supreme Court’s case-by-case application of most of the Bill of Rights to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.
Seventeenth Amendment
Ratified in 1913. Provided for the direct election of senators by voters instead of state legislatures.
Sixteenth Amendment
Ratified in 1913. Allowed a federal income tax, giving the national government the revenue that funds modern grants.
Unfunded mandate
A federal requirement that comes with little or no money to pay for it, such as many requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (1995)
Made costly unfunded mandates harder to pass by requiring cost estimates and allowing a challenge in Congress. It did not ban them.
Unitary system
A system in which the central government holds all authority and regional or local governments exist only by its choice.
United States v. Lopez (1995)
Congress exceeded its Commerce Clause power by making gun possession in a school zone a federal crime. Required case.
Welfare Reform Act (1996)
Changed welfare from a categorical grant into a block grant (TANF — Temporary Assistance for Needy Families) giving states more control. An example of devolution.
